objective: By the end of this lesson you can say when an emergency descent is needed, recite the generic immediate actions, stay inside the airplane's speed and load limits, and fly a descending 30–45° bank turn to a level-off within ACS tolerances.
why: Fire, smoke or a loss of pressurization can leave only minutes to get down. A practiced, disciplined descent gets you lower fast without breaking the airplane.

prereading.what: Emergency descents, engine fire, electrical and cabin fires.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 18, 18-8 to 18-10

prereading.what: Airspeed indicator markings and limit speeds not marked on the ASI (VA, VLE, VLO).
prereading.label: PHAK 8-9 to 8-10

prereading.what: Load factor vs bank angle, limit load factors, the Vg diagram.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-34 to 5-38

prereading.what: Decompression and why a rapid descent is needed.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-36 to 7-37

prereading.what: MAYDAY/PAN-PAN calls, 121.5 MHz, code 7700, what to say.
prereading.label: AIM 6-3-1 to 6-3-2

warmup: You smell burning insulation at 7,500 ft and smoke starts to fill the cabin. What do you want to do with your altitude, and how fast can you safely do it?

key_terms.def: A maneuver to get down as fast as possible, to a lower altitude or to the ground, without exceeding structural limits.
The first steps of an emergency checklist you do from memory, then confirm with the checklist.
Never-exceed speed. Red line. Flying faster may cause damage or structural failure.
Maximum flap extended speed. Top of the white arc.
Maximum speed with the landing gear extended. Found in the POH/AFM, not on the ASI.
Design maneuvering speed. Use it as the limit in turbulence. It goes down as weight goes down.
G loading that pushes you into the seat. Holding 30–45° of bank keeps it positive during the descent.
Forced: can't keep flying. Precautionary: could keep flying but shouldn't.
Radio words for distress and urgency, each said three times.

chunks.title: When you need an emergency descent

body.p: An emergency descent gets you down as fast as possible, either to a lower altitude or to the ground for an emergency landing [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. The goal: descend as soon and as fast as possible without exceeding any structural limits [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

head: Situation
Why get down fast
rows: Named by the AFH as a reason for the maneuver [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
The airplane may be badly damaged, may still be burning, and is expendable. Only the people matter [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
Use oxygen masks if available and start an immediate descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
The most prudent course is to land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
Main danger is hypoxia; a rapid descent is needed [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

body.p: Rapid decompression sharply shortens your time of useful consciousness [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. In a pressurized airplane with intense smoke, you may need to depressurize (if everyone has oxygen) or make an emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

callout.text: Fire, smoke, or loss of pressure: get down now, but never past the airplane's limits [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

check.q: What situations does the AFH say can call for an emergency descent?
check.a: An uncontrollable fire, a sudden loss of cabin pressurization, or any other situation that demands an immediate, rapid descent [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

body.p: Your POH/AFM Section 3 has the emergency checklists and speeds. Memorize the immediate action items; then confirm with the checklist [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]. If the AFH's generic advice ever conflicts with the manufacturer, the manufacturer wins [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
Generic emergency descent actions, unless the manufacturer says otherwise [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]:

bullets: Power to idle.
Propeller (if equipped) to low pitch / high rpm. The prop then acts as an air brake.
Gear and flaps extended as the manufacturer recommends, for maximum drag.
Roll into about 30–45° of bank to keep positive G loads.

body.p: Engine fire, first steps (unless the POH says otherwise) [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]:

bullets: Mixture to idle cutoff and fuel selector OFF to starve the fire.
Leave the ignition ON to burn the fuel left in the lines.
If the flames go out, do not restart the engine.
Thick black smoke = likely oil-fed fire; bright orange flames = likely fuel-fed. For an oil-fed fire, consider stopping the propeller.

body.p: Cabin fire: shut down the faulty system. Use the extinguisher first, then open the vents to clear smoke. If the smoke gets worse with vents open, close them at once [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

callout.text: Turning the master switch OFF kills your radios and your transponder return. Unless the fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent, think before you switch it off [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

check.q: Engine fire in a single-engine piston airplane: what do you do with the mixture, fuel selector, and ignition?
check.a: Mixture idle cutoff, fuel selector OFF, ignition left ON, unless the POH says otherwise [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

body.p: Descend at the maximum allowable airspeed for the procedure you are using. That gives more drag and a high descent rate [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. But never pass VNE, VLE or VFE, as applicable. In turbulence, also respect VA [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

head: Speed
Meaning
Where to find it
rows: Never exceed. May cause damage or structural failure [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
Max structural cruising speed; exceed only in smooth air [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]
Max speed for full control deflection or gusts without damage [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]

body.p: VA changes with weight. The PHAK example: 100 knots heavy, but only 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

callout.text: Engine fire trade-off: a fast descent might blow the fire out, but a weakened structure is the bigger worry. A slower descent puts less stress on the airplane [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

check.q: You extend the gear and flaps for the descent. Which two limit speeds now matter besides VNE?

chunks.title: Performance and limits: load factor and structure

body.p: Gear and flaps down plus idle power give maximum drag, so you can descend fast without excessive airspeed [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. A 30–45° bank keeps positive load factors (G forces) on the airplane [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
Load factor climbs fast once bank passes 45° or 50°. In a level 60° bank it is 2 G [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. That is one reason to stay in the 30–45° range and not crank it steeper.

The Vg diagram shows the safe mix of airspeed and load factor. Each airplane has its own, valid at a certain weight and altitude [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Any maneuver or gust outside the envelope can cause structural damage [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].

callout.text: Piston engines: don't prolong emergency descent practice. It can over-cool the cylinders. Once the descent is stable in training, end it [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

check.q: Why keep the bank at 30–45° during the descent?
check.a: To maintain positive load factors (G forces) on the airplane [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

body.p: Generic AFH procedure. Your POH/AFM speeds and configuration come first [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

bullets: 1. Clear the area with clearing turns before you start [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
2. Power to idle (unless prohibited). Prop control (if equipped) to low pitch / high rpm [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
3. Roll into a 30–45° bank. Fly the descent as a turn so you can check for traffic below and look for a landing area [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
4. Extend gear and flaps as the manufacturer recommends [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Lower the gear only below VLO and the flaps only below VFE [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].
5. Pitch for the maximum allowable airspeed for that configuration. Stay under VNE/VLE/VFE, and VA if it's bumpy [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
6. Run the emergency checklist after the memory items [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]. Make a radio call if appropriate [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
7. Keep track of heading, altitude and where you are. Look outside between instrument checks.
8. Start the recovery high enough to reach level flight or set up a precautionary landing safely [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

9. Lead the level-off: start before you reach the target altitude, or you will tend to overshoot it. Lead by 10 percent of the descent rate: at 1,000 fpm, start 100 feet above the target; at 2,000 fpm, 200 feet [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
10. In training, end the descent once it is stable [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. Clean up and set cruise power.

callout.text: +0 means no faster than your target. The limits (VNE, VLE, VFE) are why there is no plus side.

check.q: What are the ACS airspeed and level-off tolerances for this task?
check.a: Airspeed +0/−10 knots, and level off at the specified altitude ±100 feet (ACS PA.IX.A.S5).

head: Error
Fix
rows: Not clearing for traffic in the turn direction or descent [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Clear first; descend in a turn and look below [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Letting speed pass VNE, VLE or VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Know the limits before the flight; watch the ASI trend
Hold a constant bank; check the attitude often
Slipping or skidding in the descending turn [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Use light rudder; keep the ball centered
Pick the level-off point before you start
Lead by 10 percent of the descent rate (100 ft at 1,000 fpm) [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Prolonged practice that over-cools the engine [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Stop once the descent is stable

body.p: The AFH has no error list just for emergency descents. These come from its emergency descent guidance and its list of descending-turn errors.

check.q: Why stop the practice descent once it's stabilized in a piston airplane?
check.a: To prevent excessive cooling of the engine cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

body.p: In practice, a radio call announcing your descent can alert other aircraft [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. In a real emergency, ask for help right away. Delay has cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

bullets: Distress: start with MAYDAY, said three times. Urgency: PAN-PAN, three times [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
Use the frequency you're on. If needed, use 121.5 MHz [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
Already talking to ATC? Keep your assigned code unless told otherwise. Can't reach anyone right away? Squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
Say who you are, the problem, weather, intentions, position, altitude, fuel in minutes, and people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

body.p: SRM pulls together situational awareness, use of resources, task management and decision-making [[24:50|AFH 2-13]]. A passenger can read a checklist or watch for something you assign [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Declaring an emergency gets you extra help and priority [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

callout.text: If you must turn the master off (electrical fire), make your call first. With the master off you lose the radios and ATC loses your transponder [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

check.q: You're on flight following with an assigned code when the fire starts. Do you change to 7700?
check.a: No. Keep the assigned code while in contact with ATC unless told otherwise. Use 7700 if you can't reach anyone right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

chunks.title: Risk: altitude, terrain and where you'll land

body.p: An emergency descent may end on the ground [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Use the turn to look for a landing area, and start the recovery high enough for a safe level-off or a precautionary landing [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

bullets: Your landing choices depend on your route, your height above the ground, and any extra airspeed, which you can trade for distance or altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
Plan the approach around wind, field size and slope, and obstacles on final [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
If obstacles block the into-wind approach, an unobstructed approach may be better, whatever the wind [[24:354|AFH 18-5]].
Land as slowly as you can. Doubling groundspeed quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

callout.text: A precautionary landing is less risky than a forced landing because you have more time and still have power. Don't let wishful thinking turn one into the other [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

check.q: Why is a precautionary landing generally less hazardous than a forced landing?
check.a: You have more time to pick terrain and plan, and you can use power to fix errors [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

body.p: Collision hazards: you are dropping fast through other traffic. Descend in a turn to look below, and announce your intentions [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Clearing turns plus good scanning are the best defense [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

Configuring the airplane: extend gear and flaps per the manufacturer, below their limit speeds [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. On some airplanes, lowering gear or flaps can make a cabin smoke problem worse [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Know your POH.

Distraction: a fire or smoke grabs all your attention. Fixating on one problem pushes out more important tasks [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

callout.text: Reluctance to accept the emergency leads to delay and indecision. Act early and keep flying the airplane [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

check.q: Why might you think twice before lowering the flaps during a cabin smoke emergency?
check.a: On some airplanes, lowering gear and/or flaps can make a cabin smoke problem worse [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

scenario.title: Smoke at 7,500 feet
scenario.setup: You're on a solo cross-country at 7,500 ft MSL in a fixed-gear, high-wing trainer, talking to ATC on flight following. You smell burning insulation. Then gray smoke starts coming from behind the panel. Below you is mostly farmland, with a small airport about 12 miles ahead. Another airplane was reported a few miles away, lower than you.

questions.q: What should you try first about the smoke?
questions.a: Try to find the faulty circuit (circuit breakers, instruments, avionics, lights). If you can't find and isolate it, and conditions permit, turn the battery master and alternator switches off [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

questions.q: Before you turn the master off, what should you do with the radio?
questions.a: Tell ATC (MAYDAY or PAN-PAN) and give your intentions. With the master off you lose the radios and ATC loses your transponder [[24:358|AFH 18-9]] [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

questions.q: The smoke gets thicker. Do you stay at altitude and fly to the airport ahead?
questions.a: No. With severe smoke, use oxygen if available and start an immediate descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. With an electrical fire, the most prudent course is to land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

questions.q: How do you manage the traffic below as you start down?
questions.a: Descend in a turn so you can check below. A radio call announcing your descent alerts others [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

questions.q: You open the vents and the smoke increases. Now what?
questions.a: Close them at once. More smoke means more airflow may be feeding the fire [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

questions.q: You find a good field 2 miles away. What decides where you level off or go for a landing?
questions.a: Start the recovery high enough to reach level flight or a precautionary landing safely. Plan around wind, field size and slope, and obstacles [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

skills.do: Clear the area before starting the descent.
skills.practice: Clearing turns every time, then fly the descent as a turn and look below [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

skills.do: Set the POH/AFM configuration and airspeed for the scenario the examiner gives (e.g., fire, smoke, pressurization).
skills.practice: Before the flight, write down your airplane's emergency descent speed, VNE, VFE, VLE and VA. Fly it with your CFI calling different scenarios.

skills.do: Stay oriented, divide your attention, and plan a smooth recovery.
skills.practice: Pick a landmark and target altitude before rolling in. Call out heading and altitude every 1,000 ft.

skills.do: Hold a 30–45° bank to keep positive load factors.
skills.practice: Practice setting the bank by the horizon first, then check the attitude indicator [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

skills.do: Hold airspeed +0/−10 knots and level off at the specified altitude ±100 ft.
skills.practice: Lead the level-off by 10 percent of the descent rate [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

skills.do: Do the memory items, then complete the checklist.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the POH emergency checklists until the memory items are automatic [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].
Rehearse a MAYDAY call aloud: who, what, intentions, position, altitude, fuel, people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

skills.do: Use SRM: manage workload and use all resources.
skills.practice: Brief a passenger on how to help, and practice asking ATC for help early [[30:46|RMH 6-3]] [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

quiz.q: The main goal of an emergency descent is to:
options: Reach the nearest airport at cruise speed
Descend as fast as possible without exceeding structural limits
Descend at VY to save the engine
Glide at best glide speed for maximum range
quiz.why: Descend as soon and as rapidly as possible without exceeding structural limits [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

quiz.q: Unless the manufacturer says otherwise, where does the propeller control go?
quiz.why: Low pitch (high rpm) lets the prop act as an aerodynamic brake [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

quiz.q: What bank angle does the AFH recommend for the descent?
quiz.why: About 30–45°, to keep positive load factors [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

quiz.q: With gear and flaps extended in turbulence, which speed limits apply?
quiz.why: Don't pass VNE, VLE or VFE, as applicable, and respect VA in turbulence [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

quiz.q: Engine fire: unless the POH says otherwise, the first step is to:
options: Shut off fuel: mixture idle cutoff and fuel selector OFF
quiz.why: Shut off fuel to the engine first; leave the ignition ON [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

quiz.q: The ACS airspeed tolerance for an emergency descent is:
You're in radio contact with ATC with an assigned code when an emergency starts. AIM guidance is to:
options: Keep the assigned code unless told otherwise
quiz.why: Keep the assigned code while in contact unless instructed otherwise; use 7700 if you can't reach anyone right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

quiz.q: Why avoid long emergency descent practice in a piston airplane?
options: It can over-cool the engine cylinders
quiz.why: Prolonged practice can cause excessive cooling of the engine cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

takeaways: Fire, smoke or loss of pressurization: get down fast, within the limits.
Idle, prop forward, gear and flaps per the POH, 30–45° bank.
Fly fast but never past VNE, VLE, VFE, or VA in turbulence.
Descend in a turn to see traffic below and find a landing spot.
Memory items, then the checklist. Call for help early.
ACS: airspeed +0/−10 kt; level off ±100 ft.
cfi_notes: Have the student brief the airplane's emergency descent speed and VNE/VFE/VLE/VA before the flight. Many don't know VLE/VA are not on the ASI.
Give a scenario (engine fire, cabin smoke, depressurization) so the student has to choose the configuration, as the ACS asks (S2).
Watch for bank creeping past 45° and airspeed creeping over the target in the steep descent.
Agree before flight how simulated radio calls will be made, so a practice MAYDAY doesn't go out on a real frequency.
Ask the electrical-fire question: what do you lose when the master goes off? (radios and transponder return).
gaps: Emergency descent airspeed, flap and gear settings are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
The AFH has no common-errors list for emergency descents; the lesson's list is drawn from its emergency descent text and descending-turn errors (AFH 3-24).
Sources give no emergency-descent-specific guidance on disorientation; the lesson uses general outside-reference and situational awareness advice.
The 10 percent level-off lead comes from general descent guidance (IFH 7-50, AFH 3-21); sources don't give a lead made just for high-rate emergency descents.
Depressurization applies only to pressurized airplanes; most training airplanes will use fire or smoke scenarios.

activities.title: Which kind of fire?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap the fire it belongs to.

items.t: Mixture to idle cutoff and fuel selector OFF
Leave the ignition ON to burn the fuel left in the lines
Thick black smoke from the cowling hints it is oil-fed
First sign is usually the smell of burning insulation
Check circuit breakers, instruments, avionics and lights
Can't find the bad circuit: battery master and alternator OFF
Use the extinguisher first, then open the vents
Smoke gets worse with the vents open: close them at once

activities.title: Read the airspeed indicator
activities.intro: Tap a marking, then the speed limit it shows.

pairs.r: VNE: never exceed, damage or failure possible
VFE: fastest you may fly with flaps out
VNO: go faster only in smooth air
Caution range: smooth air only, and with care
VLE and VA: look in the POH or on placards

activities.title: Fly the emergency descent
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Clear the area for traffic, including below you
Idle power, prop to high rpm, 30–45° bank, gear and flaps per the POH
Hold the maximum allowable airspeed, under the limit speeds
Start the level-off before you reach the target altitude
Level off at the target altitude, within 100 feet

activities.title: True or false: calling for help

cards.s: MAYDAY is for distress. PAN-PAN is for urgency.
cards.why: Yes. A distress call starts with MAYDAY and an urgency call with PAN-PAN, each said three times [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

cards.s: You can't reach any ATC facility right away. The AIM says to keep squawking 1200 until you do.
cards.why: No. If you can't reach an ATC facility right away, squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

cards.s: A MAYDAY call has priority over every other call on the frequency.
cards.why: Yes. Distress calls have absolute priority, and MAYDAY commands radio silence on that frequency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

cards.s: Wait until things are clearly dangerous before asking ATC for help.
cards.why: No. Ask as soon as you have doubts. Delay has caused accidents and cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

cards.s: If you will turn the master switch off for an electrical fire, make your radio call first.
cards.why: Yes. With the master off you can't use the panel radios, and ATC loses your transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

cards.s: 121.5 MHz is always the best first choice for an emergency call.
cards.why: No. The frequency you're already using, or one ATC assigned, is preferred. Use 121.5 MHz if needed [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these situations most clearly calls for an emergency descent?
options: The weather ahead is getting worse
You are not sure of your position
Severe smoke is filling the cabin
Fuel is lower than planned, but enough to reach an airport
final_quiz.why: With severe cabin smoke, use oxygen if you have it and start an immediate descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. The others are reasons to consider a precautionary landing, not a rapid descent [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

final_quiz.q: You see thick black smoke pouring from the cowling. Your airplane has a constant-speed propeller. What does the smoke suggest?
options: A fuel-fed fire, so turn the ignition off
An oil-fed fire, so consider stopping the propeller
An electrical fire, so turn the master switch off
Carburetor ice, so apply carburetor heat
final_quiz.why: Thick black smoke points to an oil-fed fire; bright orange flames point to fuel. For an oil-fed fire, consider stopping the propeller so the engine-driven pump stops feeding the fire [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

final_quiz.q: You shut off the fuel for an engine fire in your single-engine airplane, and the flames go out. What now?
options: Restart the engine and fly to the nearest airport
Restart the engine, but only at low power
Turn the fuel back on to cool the engine
Leave the engine off and plan a forced landing
final_quiz.why: If the flames are snuffed out, don't try to restart the engine [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. Without power, a single-engine pilot has to make a forced landing [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: You descend with the engine on fire. Why might you choose a slower descent instead of the fastest one?
options: A slower descent always puts the fire out
The fire may have weakened the structure, and lower speed puts less stress on it
Slower descents keep the radios working
A fast descent over-cools the fire and makes it spread
final_quiz.why: A high-speed descent could blow out the fire, but a weakened structure is a major concern. A low-airspeed descent puts less stress on the airplane [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your fixed-gear trainer is descending in smooth air with flaps extended per the POH. Which speed is your upper limit?
final_quiz.why: With flaps out, you may not pass VFE, the top of the white arc [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. On the airspeed indicator the white arc ends long before the red line (VNE). You may pass VNO in smooth air, and VA matters in turbulence [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH lists VA as 105 knots at maximum weight. Today you are flying alone with little fuel, and the air is bumpy. What is your VA?
options: VA does not apply during a descent
final_quiz.why: VA goes down as weight goes down. The PHAK example: 100 knots heavy, only 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. In turbulence you must also respect VA during the descent [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: During the descent your bank creeps from 40° to 60°. In a coordinated level turn, what load factor does 60° of bank produce?
final_quiz.why: In a coordinated level turn at 60° of bank, the load factor is 2 G. It climbs fast once bank passes 45° or 50° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH say to fly a simulated emergency descent as a turn?
options: To check for traffic below and look for a landing area
To keep the descent rate low
So ATC radar can track you more easily
final_quiz.why: Simulated emergency descents should be made in a turn to check for other traffic below and look for a possible landing area [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner asks for an emergency descent at 120 knots and a level-off at 3,000 feet. Which result meets the ACS standards?
final_quiz.why: The ACS allows +0/−10 knots and ±100 feet, so 115 knots at 2,920 feet passes. 125 knots is too fast, 2,850 feet is 150 feet low, and 105 knots is 15 knots slow. There is no plus side because you fly the maximum allowable airspeed and never pass VNE, VLE or VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: You are descending at 1,500 feet per minute toward 3,500 feet. Using the rule of thumb to lead a level-off from a descent by 10 percent of the descent rate, where should you start the level-off?
final_quiz.why: Lead the level-off from a descent by about 10 percent of the descent rate [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. 10 percent of 1,500 fpm is 150 feet, so start at 3,500 + 150 = 3,650 feet.

final_quiz.q: You make a MAYDAY call. Which of these does the AIM list as part of a distress message?
options: The date of your last flight review
Fuel remaining in minutes and the number of people on board
The name of your flight instructor
final_quiz.why: A distress message can include who you are, the problem, weather, intentions, position, altitude, fuel remaining in minutes and people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

final_quiz.q: You lower the flaps during a severe-smoke descent, and the smoke gets thicker. What is a likely reason?
options: On some airplanes, lowering flaps can make cabin smoke worse
Flaps always feed fuel to an engine fire
The engine cylinders are cooling too fast
Lowering flaps turns off the cabin vents
final_quiz.why: On some airplanes, lowering the landing gear or flaps can aggravate a cabin smoke problem. Know your POH [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your descent ends in a field. Touching down at 60 knots groundspeed instead of 30 knots multiplies the destructive energy by about:
final_quiz.why: Doubling the groundspeed quadruples the destructive energy. Touch down at the lowest controllable airspeed you can [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].
